newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economic reforms a big question after polls.
newsitem.headline: Japan economic reforms a big question after polls.

text.p: The messy outcome of Japan's general election on Sunday leaves unanswered questions about economic policies as the nation, emerging from a lengthy slump, struggles to clear a path to future growth.

The general election -- the first since the conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lost its monopoly on power three years ago -- put the party in the driver's seat but without the clear majority that many pollsters had thought possible.

LDP Secretary-General Koichi Kato said the LDP, before the election the dominant partner in a three-way bloc with the Social Democrats and the tiny Sakigake Party, would seek to join hands with those former allies plus the fledgling Democratic Party. But some wondered how easy that could be.
"It's hard to see how they will get a majority in the Lower House and they need one in the Upper House too," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"It's not clear to me where major economic policies are going," said Feldman, citing such issues as tax reform, deregulation and provision for a rapidly ageing society.
The election was the first since irate voters in July 1993 ended the LDP's 38-year monopoly on power and instead gave a mandate to a reformist coalition.

That shocking shift brought with it reformers' pledges to cut the red tape critics says strangles businesses. Dreams of change, however, were dashed by policy deadlock as parties stumbled into a series of coalitions culminating in a bizarre alliance between the LDP and its old Socialist rivals.

Some optimists had hoped an LDP majority would help Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, expected to head the next government, end policy drift and enact the deregulation big business wants and economists say is vital.
Expectations of an LDP majority pushed up Tokyo share prices last week on hopes of political stability and reform.
Pessimists, however, doubt whether the LDP is willing -- either single-handedly or in partnership -- to take the bold initiatives many say are needed to rejuvenate the economy.

"There are two types of reform: liberalisation versus tinkering with the existing system to make things better," said Chris Calderwood, chief economist at BZW Securities. "I think the LDP is in the second camp."
Shorter term, the need for the LDP to scramble for coalition partners clouds the outlook for some concrete steps business and share market players are keen to see implemented.

An LDP-led coalition will likely go ahead with a planned rise in the three-percent sales tax to five percent from next April. But implementation could be rocky if the LDP again joins hands with the Social Democrats, some economists said.
The Social Democrats are lukewarm toward the tax hike, which was opposed during the campaign by the main opposition party, the Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), and the Communists.

The Social Democrats are also uneasy about other steps favoured by the LDP and its corporate backers -- a reform of Japan's anti-trust law to allow holding companies, cuts in corporate taxes and changes in real estate rules to boost market liquidity, said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
Also unclear is whether Japan will have an extra budget for the current fiscal year to March 1997 to prop up the economy's tentative recovery -- and pay back election promises.

Japan's economy is gradually recovering from the prolonged slump which followed the bursting of the late 1980s economic "bubble" but the improvement is patchy and has owed much to government stimulus spending and record low interest rates.
Some LDP leaders last week tossed out a figure of a five trillion yen ($45 billion) supplementary budget for 1996/97, but economists were unsure how much of this was campaign fluff.

Politicians also need to iron out the state budget for 1997/98, as well as settle the fate of proposals by politicians to trim the power of the mighty finance ministry and boost the independence of Japan's central bank.
Potentially of greater concern than the number of seats won or lost by each party, however, could well be the disaffection which kept voter turnout at a record low 59 percent.

"Voters appear to be saying that they don't expect anything from politicians, that no matter what policies they say they will implement, it doesn't make any difference," said Masaaki Higashida, a strategist at Nomura Securities Co Ltd. ($1=112 yen)
